title: Add clusters for waiting queries; add size for a hungry query
goal: Distinguish concurrency scaling from per-query sizing so a busy SQL service does not spend more while fixing the wrong bottleneck.
tag: Focused certification lesson · compute and concurrency · cycle 4, position 5
concept:
A grocery store has two different problems. A long checkout line needs more open lanes. One oversized cart needs a lane with more room and staff.

SQL warehouses have the same split. Scale out adds clusters so more independent queries run at once. Scale up gives each cluster more compute and memory, which can help a single query that spills or scans heavily. More clusters do not automatically make one slow query fast.
example: Thirty queries arrive together. One cluster can actively serve ten in the teaching model, so twenty wait. Three same-sized clusters can serve all thirty concurrently. But one query that needs 18 GB while a cluster offers 12 GB still spills; it needs a larger size or a better plan, not another identical cluster.

use_case.when: Use this distinction when dashboard or BI users report queues, when a query profile reports spill, or when cost rises after indiscriminate warehouse resizing.
use_case.example: A finance dashboard opens at 9 AM with 30 short queries while one month-end aggregation spills to disk.
use_case.decision: Add concurrency capacity when many short queries wait. Increase size or optimize SQL when one query lacks memory or compute. Separate workloads when their SLOs and cost controls differ; measure queue and spill evidence before changing either knob.

practice: Change query count, clusters, and memory demand. Predict whether the queue or the large query remains the limiting problem.
boundary: The local arithmetic uses ten query slots per cluster and one memory threshold. Real admission, scheduling, caching, I/O, serverless prediction, query shape, cluster warm-up, permissions, editions, and credits differ. No vendor warehouse or SQL ran.

product_sections.title: Snowflake: multi-cluster is a concurrency control, not a slow-query cure
product_sections.html:
A multi-cluster warehouse adds same-sized compute clusters as queries queue. Auto-scale mode uses different minimum and maximum counts. STANDARD favors responsiveness; ECONOMY waits for enough load to keep another cluster busy. Multi-cluster warehouses require Enterprise Edition or higher.

title: A worker that leaves must deregister from the next phase
goal: Use Phaser for changing participation without leaving future phases waiting for a worker that has already finished.
concept:
Three hikers agree to regroup after every trail section. One hiker is only joining the first section. If the group still counts three people at the second checkpoint, the remaining two wait forever.

A Java Phaser is a reusable checkpoint whose registered party count may change. arriveAndAwaitAdvance() arrives and waits. arriveAndDeregister() arrives and removes that party from future phases.
example: Reader, validator, and publisher synchronize after phase 0. Reader has no work in phase 1, so it arrives and deregisters. Registered parties fall from three to two. Validator and publisher can then finish phase 1 together.

use_case.when: Use a Phaser when iterative or staged work has participants that may join or leave between phases.
use_case.example: A batch pipeline has reader partitions that finish early while validation and aggregation continue through later rounds.
use_case.decision: Use CountDownLatch for one fixed countdown and CyclicBarrier for a fixed reusable party count. Choose Phaser when changing registration is the important behavior, and define timeout/termination recovery explicitly.

practice: Toggle whether the reader deregisters. Step through phase 0 and inspect the registered and unarrived counts for phase 1.
boundary: The Java replay is single-threaded bookkeeping that calls Phaser methods in a safe order; it does not create real worker races, timeouts, interruption, forceTermination, tiered phasers, ForkJoinPool blocking, or task failure recovery.

function paintPhaser(){const leaves=readerLeaves.checked,registered=leaves?2:3,arrived=2,unarrived=Math.max(0,registered-arrived),advance=unarrived===0;phaserWorld.innerHTML='

phase 0
reader + validator + publisher
reader '+(leaves?'arrives + deregisters':'leaves silently')+'
phase 1 registered
'+registered+'
two arrivals
'+unarrived+' still expected
'+(advance?'advance':'stalled')+'
';};readerLeaves.onchange=paintPhaser;paintPhaser();
questions: Reader is finished but remains registered. Two remaining workers arrive. What happens?
Phase waits for the missing third arrival
Phaser guesses reader left
Party count becomes two automatically
Registration is explicit; abandoning work does not deregister a party.
Why use arriveAndDeregister rather than arrive alone?
It removes the party from future phase counts
It cancels every worker
It increases the party count
The current arrival is recorded and later phases no longer expect that worker.
When is CountDownLatch simpler?
One fixed, one-time countdown
Participants change every phase
The barrier repeats indefinitely
A latch is clearer when no reusable or dynamic phases are needed.

steps.note: Register three parties for phase 0.

walkthrough.limit: The Java replay is single-threaded bookkeeping that calls Phaser methods in a safe order; it does not create real worker races, timeouts, interruption, forceTermination, tiered phasers, ForkJoinPool blocking, or task failure recovery.

title: A post-incident action should remove a condition, not repeat a warning
goal: Turn incident learning into owned system changes that reduce recurrence instead of relying on people to remember one more rule.
concept:
A sign saying “remember to lock the door” depends on memory every night. A door that locks itself removes the repeated decision.

Post-incident actions vary in strength. Training and runbooks help response. Detection shortens impact. Automated checks and safer interfaces prevent the same condition from crossing the boundary. Strong actions are specific, owned, tracked, and verified with evidence.
example: A deployment published a table without its required tenant filter. “Remind engineers to check filters” leaves the unsafe route open. A contract test that blocks publication when the filter is absent turns the lesson into an enforced condition. A safe publication API that always attaches the policy removes the footgun further.

use_case.when: Use this action-strength review after incidents, near misses, audit findings, and repeated manual mistakes.
use_case.example: A public data product was deployed without the row-access policy expected by its contract.
use_case.decision: Choose the strongest feasible action near the failure boundary. Keep training for judgment-heavy cases, but do not use training as the only response to a deterministic condition a system can check. Assign an owner, due date, and verification signal.

practice: Choose a corrective action and watch the next deployment path retain or remove the unsafe branch.
boundary: The action ladder is a teaching heuristic, not a probability model or compliance framework. Automation can encode the wrong rule, introduce outages, or move risk elsewhere. Human judgment, rollout, exception handling, and outcome measurement remain necessary.

title: Decide whether a tool result needs another model turn
goal: Use tool-use behavior to stop on a trusted final tool result or deliberately send evidence back to the model for synthesis.
tag: GenAI harness engineering · tool result control
concept:
A cashier can hand you a printed receipt directly. A mechanic's diagnostic report usually needs someone to explain the next step.

The OpenAI Agents SDK defaults to run_llm_again: tools run, then their results return to the model for a final response. stop_on_first_tool treats the first function-tool output as the final result. StopAtTools can stop only for named tools. A custom function can decide from all tool results.
example: An order-status tool returns a stable customer-ready object. Stopping avoids an extra model turn that might paraphrase the status. A search tool returns evidence fragments; those should go back to the model for synthesis and citations.

use_case.when: Choose behavior when function-tool output may already be the exact final contract or still needs reasoning and presentation.
use_case.example: Return a signed receipt object directly, but synthesize multiple policy-search results into a grounded explanation.
use_case.decision: Stop only when the tool output is safe, complete, typed, and suitable as the final answer. Run the model again when results need combination, explanation, redaction, or uncertainty handling. Hosted tools are processed by the model rather than this FunctionTool control.

practice: Switch between a receipt and evidence tool, then choose direct stop or another model turn. Watch which component owns the final bytes.
boundary: The local event rail does not run the Agents SDK, a model, tools, schemas, streaming, hosted tools, approvals, guardrails, or errors. The SDK sketch is unexecuted and only covers FunctionTool result routing.

title: Freeze electron motion one lightwave slice at a time
goal: Understand how attosecond band-structure videography revealed driven carrier motion and tunnelling across graphene's momentum space.
concept:
A normal camera blurs a hummingbird's wing across the whole flap. A strobe freezes one tiny slice, then many slices reconstruct the motion.

The reported experiment used few-cycle mid-infrared fields and attosecond-precision timing to image electron distributions across graphene's first Brillouin zone. It observed displacement from intraband acceleration and distortion associated with Landau–Zener–Majorana tunnelling between bands near an avoided crossing.
example: In the teaching view, the lightwave phase moves the distribution left and right. Near the crossing, the cloud stretches into an ellipse as population tunnels into the conduction band. Later scattering makes the distribution more circular again. This is a visual analogy, not the measured dataset.

use_case.when: Use the method as research evidence for strong-field quantum materials, lightwave electronics, and separating coherent motion from scattering.
use_case.example: A materials lab wants to see whether a driven carrier cloud crosses bands during one optical cycle rather than only measuring the cycle-averaged population.
use_case.decision: Treat this as a measurement-platform advance and microscopic observation, not a production transistor or commercial logic claim. Device control, stability, integration, energy, repeatability, and useful computation remain separate evidence needs.

practice: Move the lightwave phase and watch displacement and distortion change. Predict when the carrier cloud approaches the band crossing.
boundary: The SVG is an original qualitative teaching model. It does not reproduce the article's photoelectron momentum microscopy, fields, attosecond delays, distributions, Brillouin-zone geometry, scattering fits, or tunnelling probabilities.

title: A required matrix failure may cancel siblings; an experimental failure need not
goal: Use fail-fast and per-job continue-on-error deliberately so a test matrix stops waste without hiding required coverage.
concept:
Four lab tests run in parallel. If a required safety test fails, you may stop the others to save time. If an optional experiment fails, you still want the required results.

In GitHub Actions, matrix strategy.fail-fast defaults to true. A failure in a non-tolerated matrix job cancels queued and in-progress siblings. Job-level continue-on-error can mark an experimental leg as tolerated so its failure does not trigger those cancellations.
example: Node 20 on Windows is required and fails: with fail-fast true, later Linux and macOS legs can be cancelled. Node 23 is experimental and has continue-on-error: true: its failure does not cancel the required Node 20 and 22 legs.

use_case.when: Use matrix failure policy when compatibility tests run across operating systems, runtimes, regions, or deployment variants.
use_case.example: Test a Java library on supported JDK 17/21 plus an experimental JDK 26 early-access leg.
use_case.decision: Use fail-fast when one required failure makes remaining results low-value and cancellation is safe. Disable it when complete failure evidence matters. Tolerate only clearly labeled experiments; never use continue-on-error to make required coverage green.

practice: Choose which leg fails and toggle fail-fast. Watch queued siblings become cancelled or continue while experimental tolerance stays distinct.
boundary: The model assumes a fixed start order and instant failure. GitHub runner availability, already-completed jobs, cancellation latency, expressions, max-parallel, matrix expansion, billing, and step-level continue-on-error are not executed.

title: Give API errors a stable type, not a sentence clients must parse
goal: Use RFC 9457 problem details so machines branch on a documented type while people receive occurrence-specific guidance.
concept:
A hospital form has a standard diagnosis code and a note for this patient. Software needs the code; a person needs the note.

RFC 9457 defines application/problem+json. type identifies the stable problem class. title summarizes that class. detail explains this occurrence. instance identifies this occurrence. Optional status mirrors the real HTTP status and must agree when generated.
example: An order exceeds its account limit. The response is HTTP 403 with type https://api.example/problems/credit-limit, a helpful detail, and an extension availableCredit: 30. The client branches on type, never on the English detail sentence.

use_case.when: Use problem details when an HTTP API needs a reusable machine-readable error envelope beyond the status code.
use_case.example: An order API must distinguish credit-limit, inventory, and validation problems while keeping each occurrence traceable.
use_case.decision: Reuse a plain status code when it already says enough. Define a stable documented type and typed extensions when clients need more. Do not expose stack traces, SQL, secrets, account internals, or personal data in detail or instance links.

practice: Switch problem types and toggle an unsafe debug field. Inspect which fields are stable class identity, occurrence detail, and security leakage.
boundary: The model emits two synthetic problem shapes. It does not implement HTTP content negotiation, localization, authentication, caches, proxies, OpenAPI schemas, registries, dereferenceable type pages, or a security review.
